analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to get ticketed passengers to their destination and rebook them free after cancellations.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee: no hearings, no vote, and no cosponsors before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Department of Transportation to write rules making an airline ticket a firm promise: if an airline cancels your flight, it must get you to your destination at no extra cost and in a reasonable, timely way. Today US airlines may rebook stranded passengers or refund them, but no federal rule guarantees a free alternative flight on a deadline. The bill was introduced in June 2018, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers whose flights get canceled. They would be entitled to a free, timely alternative flight to their destination rather than depending on each airline's voluntary rebooking policies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the Transportation Department to require that buying a ticket guarantees transportation to the advertised destination [S2].
If a carrier cancels a flight, it would have to provide each passenger alternative transportation to that destination at no additional expense and in a reasonable and timely manner [S2].
The requirement would apply to covered air carriers and was to be written as regulations within one year of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would bear the cost of rebooking canceled passengers on their own or other flights instead of offering refunds and leaving passengers to fend for themselves. Those costs could surface in fares.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteeing free, timely rebooking after every cancellation would cost airlines money on a disruption-prone product, and some of that cost could be passed to travelers through higher fares [S3].

The bill left key terms to regulators, including what counts as a 'covered air carrier' and what 'reasonable and timely' means, so the practical protection would depend on rules the Transportation Department writes rather than the statute itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection would address a real, recurring problem: US rules currently require refunds for canceled flights but do not require airlines to get passengers to their destination, unlike the binding EU rules for the same situation. The main cost falls on airlines, which are best positioned to absorb rebooking expenses, though travelers could see some of it in fares. The bill's vagueness on carrier coverage and rebooking deadlines is a fair criticism, but those details were left for regulation by design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Tina Smith introduced the bill on June 28, 2018 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No other actions were listed before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill received no cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US airlines came out ahead: they never had to rebook canceled passengers for free under a federal deadline, and passengers retained only the weaker protections that existed before. A traveler holding a ticket for a canceled flight is still left with whatever the airline's own policy provides.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: US airlines, unaffected by rebooking mandates

for.name: Tina Smith
for.role: US Senator from Minnesota and the bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Airline Consumer Protection Act of 2018 and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Thune
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its history.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan alignment was ever tested in a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required airlines to rebook canceled passengers to their destination at no extra cost and on a timely basis, replacing refund-and-fend-for-yourself practice with a binding guarantee. Airline compliance costs are the direct price of the protection travelers would gain.
